title: Why you have to shuffle a deck 7 times
description:
Number a deck 1 to 52 and riffle it once: each half keeps its order, so the deck is just two climbing runs woven together (1, 2, 3... into 27, 28, 29...). Every riffle can at most double the runs: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, while a random deck has about 26. Measured as distance from random (total variation), 4 riffles are still at 100%, 5 at 92%, 6 at 61%, 7 at 33%, and each riffle after that roughly halves it. Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis proved this in 1992, which is why 7 riffles is the standard answer.

Numbers checked in code: the exact Bayer-Diaconis formula for 52 cards (7 riffles: 0.334), plus 100,000 simulated riffles and 100,000 random decks for the run counts. Sources: Wikipedia, Shuffling and Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model.

social_caption: Your deck isn't shuffled until you riffle it 7 times. Here's how to see the order hiding in a 3-riffle deck.
facts_checked: Bayer and Diaconis (1992): the deck did not start to become random until five good riffle shuffles, and was truly random after seven; GSR model fits human riffles (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuffling)
Seven riffles give total variation distance 0.334 for 52 cards; five leave it close to one (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert%E2%80%93Shannon%E2%80%93Reeds_model)

Exact distance from random after k riffles, Bayer-Diaconis formula C(2^k + 52 - r, 52) / 2^(52k) over rising sequences r: 4 -> 1.000, 5 -> 0.924, 6 -> 0.614, 7 -> 0.334, 8 -> 0.167, 9 -> 0.085, 10 -> 0.043 (verify.py)
One riffle leaves at most 2 rising runs, 3 riffles at most 8 (2^k); a random 52-card deck has 26.5 runs on average; 5 riffles is the first with room for 26 (verify.py, simulated 100,000 decks each)

beats.say: Your deck isn't shuffled until you riffle it 7 times.
Three riffles look random. They're nowhere close.
Number your cards 1 to 52, in order. Cut the deck and riffle the halves together.
Each half keeps its order. So your deck is just two climbing runs. 1, 2, 3, woven into 27, 28, 29.
Riffle again: at most 4 runs. Then 8, 16, 32.
A truly random deck has about 26 runs. So is 5 riffles enough?
Measure how far your deck is from random. Five riffles: 92%. Six: 61%. Seven: 33%. Then each riffle halves what's left.
The drop comes all at once, and it lands at seven. Dave Bayer and Persi Diaconis proved it in 1992.
